title: Visiting the sick
hookLine: no harm, a purification, if Allah wills (Bukhari)
tomorrow: someone sneezes mid-visit. is there a right thing to say?

cards: The hospital door is half open. There's a beeping machine, a tray of food nobody touched, and someone you love looking smaller than usual in a gown. You hover in the doorway holding a card.
Everything you rehearsed sounds wrong now. Get well soon feels thin. Everything happens for a reason feels worse.

Al-Bukhari keeps a scene for exactly this doorway. The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, visits a sick man, a Bedouin, and says a few short words: no harm, a purification, if God wills. And the man argues back.

teach.h: SAY THE HOPEFUL THING, THEN LISTEN.
teach.b: A purification, says the Bedouin? No. It's a fever boiling in an old man, and it will take him to the grave.
And the Prophet answers: then so it is. He doesn't win the point. The words of comfort are offered, not forced, and the sick man's own account is allowed to stand.
That's the first lesson of the room: say the hopeful thing, then listen. Now the debate, and it's a real one. Is visiting the sick a duty, or a strongly urged kindness?

One view: a duty. The Prophet told his followers to feed the hungry, visit the sick and free the captive, in the form of a command, and al-Bukhari himself names a chapter for the obligation of visiting the sick.

teach.h: VIEW TWO: STRONGLY URGED, ON THE COMMUNITY.
teach.b: The other view: it's urged so strongly that a community must see it done, but not every person sins by missing one visit; someone goes, and the duty is met. Both views send people through that doorway.
Neither treats it as optional in spirit. And here's why. In a hadith in Sahih Muslim, God says on the last day: I was sick and you did not visit Me.
How could You be sick? the person asks.

teach.h: YOU WOULD HAVE FOUND ME WITH HIM.
teach.b: And God answers: had you visited him, you would have found Me with him.
Christians know a close neighbor of this line, from Matthew's Gospel: "I was sick, and ye visited me."

how: Muslims visit the sick at home and in hospitals, often saying the Prophet's words from al-Bukhari, la ba's, tahurun in sha Allah: no harm, a purification, if God wills.

o: a prayer recited only at the bedside of the dying
sending money to a hospital in someone's name
going to see someone who is ill, a deed strongly urged

games.q: who said what in the room — tap the pairs.
p: a fever that will take me
visiting the sick is a duty
urged, on the community as a whole

s: the Prophet corrected the sick man when he argued back
he answered: then so it is. comfort was offered, not forced.
a hadith has God say: I was sick and you did not visit Me
in Sahih Muslim: had you visited him, you would have found Me with him.
visiting the sick only counts if you say the Arabic words
the words are the Prophet's own comfort; the visit itself is what's urged.

games.q: your friend says visiting the sick is a strict duty for every Muslim, every time. she asks for the best case for the other view. what do you give her?
o: it's just a nice extra; the Prophet never really told anyone to do it.
it's urged so strongly the community must see it done, and when someone goes, the duty is met.
visiting doesn't help the patient, so it can't be a duty.
games.why: that's the strongest form of the second view. the first view points to the command to visit the sick and al-Bukhari's chapter on its obligation. both send people through the door.

practice: Think of one person who is unwell right now, in body or in spirit. Write them a short message, three or four plain lines, no advice. You can send it after the sit, or keep it as a version until it feels right.

wordCard.voice: Visiting the sick. In Arabic, 'iyadat al-marid: going to someone who is ill, a deed so urged that scholars debate whether it's a duty.

orig.note: Arabic: tahur, a purification. From the visit: la ba's, tahurun in sha Allah.

carryVoice: Hold onto this: a purification, offered gently, and then you listen. Day thirteen of fourteen remembrances.

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 3616 (also 5656): the Prophet visits a sick Bedouin, 'no harm, a purification, if God wills'
Sahih al-Bukhari 5649 (feed the hungry, visit the sick, free the captive); Kitab al-Marda, chapter on the obligation of visiting the sick
Sahih Muslim 2569 (I was sick and you did not visit Me)

sources.q: I was sick, and ye visited me
